content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a biologically-inspired defense called R-Blur. R-Blur is a pre-processing operation. It uses adaptive Gaussian kernels to blur the input and reduce its color saturation adaptively according to the pixel’s distance from a fixation pixel. R-Blur outperforms existing biologically-inspired defenses and achieves closer robustness to non-biological defenses. Moreover, R-Blur can be a certified defense using the randomized smoothing technique.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The idea of using a baiologically-inspired technique to improve adversarial robustness is very interesting. The resulting proposed method is novel. The motivation and the rationale behind the proposed method are clear and reasonable.

2. Compared to existing biologically-inspired defenses, the proposed R-Blur achieves good robustness. It is an effective method.

3. In addition to empirical robustness, this paper considers certified robustness as well. The proposed R-Blur can extend to a certified defense, which is impressive.

4. This paper conducts a good ablation study. It detailedly analyzes all the components’ contributions, making the proposed method’s effectiveness more convincing.


Weaknesses / Questions / Suggestions:

1. Parts of the experimental setup are not clear

(a) In Sec. 3.1, what are the exact operations of G-Noise and R-Warp? As main baselines, brief descriptions for them are needed. If they are already explained in previous sections, please explicitly indicate that (I cannot clearly find that) or cite properly.

(b) How many fixation points are sampled for each input image at training time? How do the sampling numbers affect model performance?

(c) There is a total of 10,000 test images in CIFAR-10. Why are only 1,000 images used for evaluation? This makes the experimental results less convincing.

(d) The first paragraph of Sec. 3.1 only describes Ecoset-10 dataset, but the second paragraph suddenly mentions Ecoset-100. This is confusing.

(e) The APGD attack is used for evaluating adversarial robustness (Sec. 3.2). A brief description of APGD should be contained in Sec. 3.1, and the reference should be cited.

2. Is the adversarial robustness evaluated under the white-box setting (i.e., is the attacker aware of the pre-processing operation?)? Furthermore, simply G-Noise can improve robustness, which is unexpected. I’m not pretty sure what G-Noise is (as I ask in point 1a). If it is just adding Gaussian noises into the input image at the pre-processing stage, it should not be robust against white-box attacks [r1]. The authors should provide an explanation of this point.

3. Since the proposed method is a pre-processing operation, it would increase training and inference costs. What is the computational cost of the proposed method? Quantitative results about its effect on training and inference costs should be provided.

4. The robustness of the proposed R-Blur is still much lower than adversarial training (AT). R-Blur achieves closer robust accuracy to AT only when the perturbation size (epsilon) is very small. Most adversarial robustness paper uses L_inf epsilon=0.016 (8/255) for evaluation. However, under epsilon=0.016, R-Blur has only around 20% accuracy. In contrast, AT achieves around 50%. This is actually still a big gap.

An idea in my mind is combining AT. R-Blur and AT are two complementary techniques. Can we combine these two to achieve better robustness?

5. R-Blur sacrifices clean accuracy to a larger extent compared to the other methods, which is a big issue. Can we have an adaptive mechanism that balances the trade-off between clean and robust accuracy? A related idea can be found in [r2], which identifies the input type and uses the corresponding strategy. [r2] is just a reference showing the idea. There should be a better way for this paper.

6. Minor typos

(a) Sec. 2.3 Line 4: “The the acuity of” -> “The acuity of”

(b) Sec. 2.4 Line 5: “the pixels assigned to these bins k bins ahead” -> “the pixels assigned to these k bins ahead”

(c) Sec. 3.1 Line 2: “subset of Ecoset Mehrer et al. (2021)” -> “subset of Ecoset (Mehrer et al., 2021)”

7. For the papers which have been published in a conference or a journal, they should be cited accordingly (instead of citing them as arXiv).

[r1] Raff, Edward, et al. "Barrage of random transforms for adversarially robust defense." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2019.
[r2] S.-Y. Lo and V. M. Patel, “Defending Against Multiple and Unforeseen Adversarial Videos,” in IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, 2021.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose a simple yet effective biologically inspired defense method for classification networks against adversarial attacks. They simulate the peripheral vision of humans, specifically the loss in contrast and color sensitivity of human perception with increasing eccentricity. The Gaussian blur intensity increases along the distance to the fixation point, and the color saturation decreases. They call this technique R-Blur (retina-blur) and apply it to the preprocessing of the images during the training of networks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

The method seems to be a smart trick inspired by the biological structure of the fovea, and it seems to work out of the box. The results show that such defense methods are effective and can achieve certified adversarial robustness.

The method is easy to implement and reproduce. It does not cost much more additional computation to perform Gaussian blurring, or de-saturation to preprocess an image. They can run much faster if parallelism is implemented such as fused CUDA kernels, even though the authors did not seem to attempt this in the paper.

**Weaknesses**
The motivation is that by simulating human eye fovea the network may be robust against some adversarial attacks. However, to me, human eyes' robustness does not seem to come from the fovea structure, and the vulnerability of deep networks does not seem to be caused by lacking resemblance to a biological vision system. For example, what is the end of biology resemblance? If we simulate a perfect fovea and create such a dataset, will the model still be vulnerable to adversarial attacks? It seems that the network architecture also plays a role; preprocessing the input images can only solve part of the problem.

The attention mechanism in some networks may have a similar effect and it is also inspired by biology. Does that mean it naturally has some robustness? I would first start with such existing architectures to study their robustness. This is also related to the previous point.

The method and experiments are mostly empirical, not involving much theoretical contribution. This means it is difficult to extend the conclusions beyond the scope of this paper; for example, does it also work for other tasks, such as object detection? Does it apply to larger datasets, such as ImageNet? Does it work for other architectures such as transformer-based architectures? I encourage the authors to do such experiments to show it generalizes to the latest architectures and datasets.

Some minor problems due to empirical nature of the paper; for example, the fixation point choice is somewhat arbitrary: 
>  For the preprocessing of R-Blur and R-Warp, we sample the fixation point uniformly at random during training and, during inference, we average the logits for 5 predefined fixation points. These points are (h/6, w/6), (h/6, w − w/6), (h/2, w/2), (h − h/6, w/6), (h − h/6, w − w/6), where h and w are the height and width of the image.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Novelty**
In the adversarial attack and defense space, the idea can be considered novel. 

**Quality**
The paper is well written. The method and experiments are mostly empirical.

**Reproducibility**
Seems reproducible, as the method is simple to implement.
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors did extensive studies on their method and prove that such defense is practical and effective. My biggest concern is that the contribution is mostly empirical; it hardly inspires us (readers) to invent something new beyond what is covered in this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new biologically inspired defense method, R-Blur, against adversarial attack. Its main idea is to pre-process the input images, in a manner where the pixels are blurred according to their distance to some selected fixation points and their color saturation reduced accordingly. In R-Blur, only a small region of pixels around the fixation points is preserved high-fidelity details, and other pixels only keep low-fidelity information. In this way, adversarial perturbations, which only perturb the images slightly to keep their semantic meaning, is on longer so effective at changing model predictions. Experiments on Cifar-10 and Ecoset-10(100) validate the effectiveness of the proposed R-Blur.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The idea is novel. R-Blur is an elegantly designed biologically inspired image processing method. Keeping only most information around certain points works much like human visual attention mechanism.
2. The writing is good. The motivation of R-Blue is cleared described from a biology perspective.
3. The robustness of R-Blur is thoroughly evaluated using both empirical metric and certified metric.

Weakness:
1. My main concern is about the performance of R-Blur, including both accuracy and inference speed. Even though R-Blur outperforms another biological defense method R-Warp significantly, it is still worse than adversarial training on both clean images and adversarially perturbed images. In my opinion, R-Blur is already a good and solid step toward a defense mechanism more aligned with human vision, so putting too much weight on comparing with the state-of-the-art performer may not be necessary. But the current R-Blur version involves in the ensemble of the predictions of 5 predefined fixation points. This will make the inference speed 5x slower, undermining the practical value of R-Blur, and make one wonder if similar robustness can be achieved by simply using the average predictions from 5 differently randomly augmented input images with advanced image transformation techniques?
2. Also, I wonder if it is plausible to dynamically select the fixation points based on the input, similar to the attention mechanism, instead of using pre-defined fixation points. This way it works more similar to human vision system.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The idea is novel and solid with a biological model. The writing is good and the method is well-presented. In general, I find reading this paper rather enjoyable.
content.summary_of_the_review: I would like to recommend acceptance given the idea of R-Blur is novel and with solid biological model proof. But my concerns about performance and fixation points selection (listed in the weakness part) hold me back. Right now my rating is marginally below the acceptance threshold, but I am happy to change my rating if the authors can list convincing evidence why they shouldn't be concerns.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a biologically-inspired defense by training along with low-fidelity images. The presented R-Blur preprocesses inputs by Gaussian noise and adaptive blurring. The method is claimed to mitigate weak adversarial attacks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
+ The pre-processing method is computationally friendly.
+ The proposed method is certifiable.

Weakness
+ The method could only mitigate small-radius adversarial attacks, and the overall defense performance is weak.
+ The method significantly hurt the clean accuracy (as a pre-processing defense).
+ Although the authors mention lots of biologically inspired defenses, the experiments only compare with R-Warp and G-noise. The lack of compared baselines makes the experiments weak.
+ The organization of Section 2 is confusing. It would be better to disentangle the analysis from the steps of the algorithm.
+ The method is complex and includes lots of heuristic factors. It is unclear how the large number of hyper-parameters affects the final performance.
+ Could the proposed method aid existing non-biological defenses?
+ The selection of the fixation point is random instead of focusing on the key parts, so Fig. 1 is confusing on this.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although biological-inspired defense is interesting, the current version is not ready for publication in terms of defense performance, experimental design, and paper presentation.

content.title: Less Is More: Training on Low-Fidelity Images Improves Robustness to Adversarial Attacks
content.abstract: Since adversarial attacks are defined relative to human perception, it may be fruitful to investigate why human perception (and biological perception in general) is robust to the types of perturbations that DNNs are convincingly deceived by. In the context of vision, we hypothesize that a factor contributing to the robustness of human visual perception is our constant exposure to low-fidelity visual stimuli. To investigate the impact, vis-à-vis adversarial robustness, of exposure to low-fidelity visual stimuli, we train and evaluate object recognition DNNs on images which have been blurred and have had their color saturation reduced. We find that DNNs trained on such images can achieve high classification accuracy over a small number of classes, while becoming significantly more robust to low-magnitude adversarial attacks. Furthermore, we design a blurring module that simulates that loss of visual acuity with increasing eccentricity by selecting the intensity of Gaussian blur at each pixel based on its distance from a given fixation point. Our results indicate that using this retina-inspired blurring mechanism, instead of blurring the entire image with the same Gaussian kernel, yields better robustness while keeping the accuracy on clean data unchanged.
